abstract: We study the problem of aligning data from multiple modalities into a shared
  representation space, focusing on settings where strong pretrained unimodal encoders
  are available but cross-modal paired data are scarce. We propose a structure-preserving
  alignment framework, joint kernel entropic Gromov--Wasserstein Optimal Transport
  (JK-EGW), which maps multiple modalities into a common latent space by minimizing
  a quadratic optimal transport objective. JK-EGW leverages fine-grained similarity
  relationships within and across modalities to construct a global affinity kernel
  instead of relying on raw feature-space distances. Our framework naturally provides
  explicit control over the geometry and distribution of the latent embedding. On
  the theory side, we establish parametric sample complexity rate of $n^-1/2$, matching
  the corresponding rates for standard, entropic and Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport.
  On the algorithmic side, we derive a scalable alternating procedure to solve JK-EGW
  with entropic optimal transport (EOT) updates through a low-rank kernel approximation
  and a variational lifting. This lifting scheme effectively relieves the burden of
  a quadratic objective, and allowing us to take the advantage of existing EOT solvers.
  Empirically, we focus on post-hoc alignment of embeddings from pretrained encoders
  in data-scarce regimes, and show that our proposed method achieves improved multimodal
  retrieval performance compared to existing alignment baselines.

You turn a paper into `studies/wu-2026-multimodal/extraction.json`, the list every implementer and reviewer works from. You do not write solver code.

**Input:** the PDF at `papers/wu-2026-multimodal.pdf`. It is gitignored. If it is missing, stop and say so. Also read `studies/wu-2026-multimodal/paper.yaml` and `studies/wu-2026-multimodal/problem/setup.py` to see which experiment is being reproduced.

**Write one item per implementable fact:**
- `method`: an algorithm or numerical method the paper uses (one item per algorithm, including its pseudocode figure)
- `equation`: governing equations, estimators, update rules, discretisations, boundary formulas
- `parameter`: every setting a run needs (problem sizes, thresholds, particle counts, seeds, tolerances)
- `boundary_condition`
- `result`: a table or figure we compare against

Each item has `id` (kebab-case, stable), `kind`, `text` (your plain statement), `page` (the printed page number, or the PDF page for preprints without one), `quote` (a short verbatim excerpt, 30 words at most) and `missing: false`.

**Gaps:** when an implementer would need a detail the paper does not give (a convergence tolerance, an initial condition, a definition left to another paper, a dataset that is not named), add an item with `missing: true`, the page where the detail belongs, `quote: ""`, and an `assumption` giving the default you recommend and why. Never fill a gap silently inside `text`.

Fill in its page fields (any key named `page` or `page_*`) and set `verified_against_pdf: true` only if every number matches. List every mismatch in your final message, and do not change any reference value without listing it.

Set `extractor_agent` to an identifier of yourself (`tool:role`, e.g. `claude-code:raft-extractor`).

  "title": "Extraction: implementable facts from a paper, each with a page",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "required": ["study", "items"],
  "properties": {
    "study": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
    "extractor_agent": {"type": "string"},
    "items": {
      "type": "array",
      "minItems": 1,
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "additionalProperties": false,
        "required": ["id", "kind", "text", "page", "quote", "missing"],
        "properties": {
          "id": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$"},
          "kind": {"enum": ["method", "equation", "parameter", "boundary_condition", "result"]},
          "text": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
          "page": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1},
          "quote": {"type": "string"},
          "missing": {"type": "boolean"},
          "assumption": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1}

        "if": {"properties": {"missing": {"const": true}}},

}
{
  "study": "transduced-lm-2026",
  "extractor_agent": "claude-code:raft-extractor",
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "target-prefix-probability",
      "kind": "equation",
      "text": "Estimand. For a source LM p_X over X* and a transducer f: X* -> Y*, the target prefix probability is Z = p_Y->(y) = Pr_{X~p_X}[y ⪯ f(X)] = sum_x 1{y ⪯ f(x)} p_X(x) (Eq. 3). Source prefix probability p_X->(x) = sum_{x'} p_X(x x'); conditionals p_X->(x'|x) = p_X->(x x')/p_X->(x) and p_X->(EOS|x) = p_X(x)/p_X->(x) (Eq. 1). p_X(x) = p_X->(EOS|x) prod_t p_X->(x_t|x_<t).",
      "page": 3,
      "quote": "A transduced language model is a language model pY characterized by the tuple (pX, f) where f is a transducer encoding a function f: X* → Y*.",
      "missing": false
    },
    {
      "id": "zero-mass-convention",
      "kind": "boundary_condition",
      "text": "When p_X->(x) = 0 take p_X->(x'|x) = 0 and p_X->(EOS|x) = 1. A remainder summand is defined to be zero when p_X->(EOS|x) = 0 (its contribution to A is then zero).",
      "page": 3,
      "quote": "When p⃗X(x) = 0, we take p⃗X(x′ | x) = 0 and p⃗X(EOS | x) def= 1.",
      "missing": false
    },
    {
      "id": "quotient-remainder-decomposition",
      "kind": "equation",
      "text": "Precover P(y) = {x : y ⪯ f(x)}; C(y) = largest union of cylinders <x> contained in P(y); quotient Q(y) = pf(C(y)) (prefix-free generators); remainder R(y) = P(y) \\ C(y). Then p_Y->(y) = sum_{x in R(y)} p_X(x) + sum_{x in Q(y)} p_X->(x) (Eq. 4). Every source string is counted exactly once.",
      "page": 3,
      "quote": "The quotient and remainder are Q(y) def= pf(C(y)) and R(y) def= P(y) \\ C(y). The computational shortcut is the quotient–remainder decomposition",
      "missing": false
    },
    {
      "id": "precover-predicates",
      "kind": "equation",
      "text": "The algorithms touch the transducer only through three predicates: is_live(x,y): some extension x x' is in P(y); is_member(x,y): x in P(y) (output so far covers y); is_cylinder(x,y): every extension covers y. 1	                                               Multimodal Alignment Through Joint Kernel Entropic
2	                                                     Gromov–Wasserstein Optimal Transport
3	
4	                                          Yixuan Florence Wu                                                yixuanwu@u.northwestern.edu
5	                                          Department of Engineering Sciences and Applied Mathematics
6	                                          Northwestern University
7	                                          Evanston, IL 60208, USA
8	                                          Yilun Zhu                                                                    allanzhu@umich.edu
9	                                          Deparment of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
10	                                          University of Michigan
11	                                          Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA
12	                                          Naichen Shi                                                naichen.shi@northwestern.edu
13	                                          Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences
14	
15	
16	
17	
18	arXiv:2608.04234v1 [math.ST] 4 Aug 2026
19	                                          Department of Mechanical Engineering
20	                                          Northwestern University
21	                                          Evanston, IL 60208, USA
22	
23	
24	                                                                                        Abstract
25	                                              We study the problem of aligning data from multiple modalities into a shared representation
26	                                              space, focusing on settings where strong pretrained unimodal encoders are available but cross-
27	                                              modal paired data are scarce. We propose a structure-preserving alignment framework, joint
28	                                              kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein Optimal Transport (JK-EGW), which maps multiple
29	                                              modalities into a common latent space by minimizing a quadratic optimal transport objective.
30	                                              JK-EGW leverages fine-grained similarity relationships within and across modalities to
31	                                              construct a global affinity kernel instead of relying on raw feature-space distances. Our
32	                                              framework naturally provides explicit control over the geometry and distribution of the
33	                                              latent embedding. On the theory side, we establish parametric sample complexity rate of
34	                                              n−1/2 , matching the corresponding rates for standard, entropic and Gromov–Wasserstein
35	                                              optimal transport. On the algorithmic side, we derive a scalable alternating procedure to
36	                                              solve JK-EGW with entropic optimal transport (EOT) updates through a low-rank kernel
37	                                              approximation and a variational lifting. This lifting scheme effectively relieves the burden
38	                                              of a quadratic objective, and allowing us to take the advantage of existing EOT solvers.
39	                                              Empirically, we focus on post-hoc alignment of embeddings from pretrained encoders in
40	                                              data-scarce regimes, and show that our proposed method achieves improved multimodal
41	                                              retrieval performance compared to existing alignment baselines.
42	                                              Keywords: Kernel Gromov–Wasserstein Optimal Transport, Multimodal Alignment,
43	                                              Finite-rank Approximation, Sample Complexity, Representation Learning
44	
45	
46	                                          1 Introduction
47	                                          Multimodal learning aims to integrate information from heterogeneous data sources, such
48	                                          as images, text, audio, and sensor measurements. Since different modalities are often
49	                                          represented in distinct feature spaces, a fundamental challenge is to construct a shared
50	                                          representation in which semantically related observations from different modalities become
51	                                          comparable (Wang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Such aligned represen-
52	
53	                                          ©2026 Yixuan Florence Wu, Yilun Zhu, Naichen Shi.
54	                                          License: CC-BY 4.0, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.
55	                                      Wu, Zhu, and Shi
56	
57	
58	
59	
60	tations provide a common interface for downstream tasks (Liang et al., 2024), including
61	cross-modal retrieval (Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015; Faghri et al., 2017), zero-shot classifica-
62	tion (Frome et al., 2013; Radford et al., 2021), multimodal prediction (Liang et al., 2021),
63	and representation transfer (Moschella et al., 2022), etc. Developing principled methods
64	for multimodal alignment is therefore a basic step toward learning systems that can use
65	complementary information across modalities.
66	    A large number of techniques focus on pretraining joint representation encoders via
67	auto-encoders (Suzuki et al., 2016; Sutter et al., 2024), contrastive learning (Radford et al.,
68	2021; Elizalde et al., 2023), and auto-regressive learning (Team et al., 2024; Aiello et al.,
69	2024). To circumvent the need for extensive training data and computational resources,
70	numerous methods (Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Gröger et al., 2025) also propose to
71	leverage pretrained single-modal encoders, such as DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025), Modern-
72	BERT (Warner et al., 2025), or BEATs (Chen et al., 2022), to construct semantically aligned
73	representations across modalities. We focus on this setting of representation alignment.
74	    One limitation of these approaches, however, is that the distribution of the joint represen-
75	tations remains uncontrolled. The geometry of the shared space is largely determined from
76	the source encoders and shaped by the alignment objective, without being explicitly matched
77	to a prescribed reference distribution. Consequently, the learned representations may exhibit
78	undesirable geometric properties, such as anisotropy, distortions, or even mode collapse.
79	This motivates our central research question: can we construct joint latent representations
80	that preserve semantic structure from multiple modalities while conforming to a prescribed
81	marginal distribution?
82	    We address this question from the perspective of Gromov–Wasserstein optimal transport
83	(GWOT) (Mémoli, 2011). GWOT constructs a probabilistic coupling between distributions
84	supported on distinct spaces by minimizing the discrepancy between their within-space
85	pairwise relations. The resulting coupling therefore aligns the two distributions by preserving,
86	as closely as possible, the relational structure of the source representations.
87	    It is therefore natural to extend the standard GWOT formulation (Peyré et al., 2016)
88	to multimodal representation learning. Such an extension should integrate two types of
89	information. The first is the semantic structure of the observed features within each
90	modality, which should be preserved when modality-specific knowledge is transferred to the
91	joint representation space. The second is the set of cross-modal correspondences, which
92	characterizes the relationships among observations from different modalities and guides their
93	alignment in the joint space.
94	    To capture both sources of information, we construct a global affinity kernel K on the
95	disjoint union of all modality-specific representation spaces. Consider, for example, an
96	image–text alignment problem. Within the image modality, an image of a black dog may
97	have high affinity with another image of a black dog. Across modalities, the same image
98	may also have high affinity with the text “black dog” (see Figure 1). More generally, we
99	propose to construct the within-modality component of K by feature similarity metrics, and
100	the cross-modality component of K by domain knowledge, including class labels (Cristianini
101	et al., 2001), expert knowledge (Kulis et al., 2005), or similarities derived from pretrained
102	representations (Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018).
103	    Building on this affinity kernel, we introduce the joint kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein
104	(JK-EGW) objective, which formulates joint representation learning as an optimal transport
105	
106	                                               2
107	                            JK-EGW for Multimodal Alignment
108	
109	
110	
111	
112	Figure 1: A global affinity kernel K scores observation pairs within and across modalities.
113	          Each modality is coupled to a prescribed latent reference ν.
114	
115	
116	
117	problem. JK-EGW aligns the distribution of each modality with a common reference
118	distribution in the latent space through probabilistic couplings. The objective encourages
119	observations with high affinity to link to nearby latent representations, thereby unifying
120	within-modality structure preservation and cross-modal alignment.
121	    In practical applications, instance-level cross-modal pairs are costly to collect and are
122	therefore often scarce. It is thus important to characterize the finite-sample statistical error of
123	JK-EGW. Establishing such guarantees is challenging, however, because the general GWOT
124	objective takes the form of a nonconvex quadratic program (Scetbon et al., 2022), whose
125	global optimization can be NP-hard (Burkard, 1984; Kravtsova, 2024). This nonconvexity
126	complicates the statistical analysis and the optimization of empirical solutions.
127	    We address this challenge by studying a specific class of kernel GWOT problems whose
128	affinity kernel K approximately admits a separable decomposition in terms of products of
129	basis functions. For a finite-rank truncation of K, we show that the resulting quadratic
130	GWOT problem can be lifted to a linear optimal transport (LOT) problem whose cost
131	function depends on an additional set of auxiliary variables. This reformulation makes
132	the statistical error amenable to analysis using tools developed for LOT. In particular, we
133	establish finite-sample guarantees showing that the empirical optimal value converges to
134	its population counterpart at the parametric rate O(n−1/2 ). For the full-kernel objective,
135	the bound includes an additional truncation term that quantifies the discrepancy between
136	the original kernel and its finite-rank approximation. Our results therefore distinguish the
137	statistical error arising from finite sampling from the approximation error introduced by
138	kernel truncation.
139	    Computationally, the basis-product structure naturally motivates an efficient alternating
140	optimization algorithm for JK-EGW. We first construct a low-rank approximation of the
141	empirical kernel matrix and use it to derive a variational lifting of the original quadratic
142	objective. The lifted optimization problem should optimize over both the transport plan
143	and the auxiliary variables. With fixed transport plan, the auxiliary variables admit a
144	closed-form update. With fixed auxiliary variables, the transport-plan update reduces to
145	
146	                                                3
147	                                     Wu, Zhu, and Shi
148	
149	
150	
151	
152	a standard entropic optimal transport (EOT) problem over discrete distributions. The
153	latter can therefore be solved using existing scalable OT solvers, such as Sinkhorn-type
154	algorithms (Cuturi, 2013). Therefore, we can construct an alternating minimization algorithm
155	by iteratively update the two parameter blocks.
156	    We evaluate JK-EGW on image–text alignment tasks derived from MS–COCO (Lin et al.,
157	2014). The results show that JK-EGW learns geometrically coherent shared representations
158	and achieves decent performance in bidirectional image–text retrieval.
159	    In summary, our main contributions are as follows:
160	  1. We formulate joint kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein optimal transport (JK-EGW)
161	     for aligning observations from multiple modalities into a shared representation space
162	     whose marginal distribution follows a prescribed reference distribution.
163	  2. For kernels admitting a separable basis decomposition, we establish a finite-sample
164	     error bound of JK-EGW consisting of a statistical term of order O(n−1/2 ) and a
165	     kernel-truncation term. Our analysis introduces a new variational formulation and
166	     develops techniques for establishing the regularity of optimal transport plans under
167	     costs induced by the kernel basis.
168	  3. Building on the variational formulation of the empirical JK-EGW problem, we develop
169	     a scalable alternating optimization algorithm. One parameter block admits a closed-
170	     form update, while the other reduces to an entropic optimal transport (EOT) problem
171	     that can be solved using standard EOT solvers.
172	  4. We empirically evaluate JK-EGW on digit multi-feature alignment, image–text retrieval
173	     tasks to demonstrate its applicability.
174	
175	1.1 Related Works
176	Alignment of pretrained unimodal encoders. Multiple works leverage frozen pre-
177	trained unimodal encoders and learn only a lightweight post-hoc alignment mechanism
178	from scarce cross-modal correspondence data. Early works, such as APE (Rosenfeld et al.,
179	2022) and ImageBind (Girdhar et al., 2023), align several modalities onto a fixed, pre-
180	trained image–text embedding space by minimizing InfoNCE loss. Recent vision–language
181	alignment methods further develop this idea by assessing or selecting compatible frozen
182	encoder pairs and training simple projectors or alignment layers between their embedding
183	spaces (Maniparambil et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). More directly related to our empirical
184	baselines, CSA (Li et al., 2025) maps frozen unimodal features into a multimodal feature
185	space and uses a weighted similarity score. STRUCTURE (Gröger et al., 2025) improves
186	limited-data alignment by regularizing the learned representation to preserve the multiscale
187	neighborhood geometry of pretrained unimodal latent spaces. Together, these methods show
188	that post-hoc alignment of frozen encoders is a practical and data-efficient alternative to
189	training multimodal models from scratch. Our work follows a similar rationale but studies a
190	different formulation of this aligning problem, which allows for an explicitly chosen marginal
191	distribution on the shared latent space. Prior work suggests that latent geometry influences
192	compositional and cross-modal generation (Girdhar et al., 2023), robustness to missing or
193	noisy modalities (Tsai et al., 2018), downstream task performance (Jiang et al., 2023), and
194	the emergence and impact of modality gaps (Liang et al., 2022).
195	
196	                                              4
197	                          JK-EGW for Multimodal Alignment
198	
199	
200	
201	
202	Structure-aware alignment via optimal transport. Optimal transport (OT) provides
203	a distributional framework for aligning heterogeneous datasets through learned couplings.
204	Several works have used OT to improve multimodal or cross-domain alignment by exploiting
205	structure beyond independent instance matching. For example, hierarchical OT leverages
206	clustered structure to improve alignment in noisy or ambiguous settings (Lee et al., 2019),
207	while MuLOT uses self-attention for intra-modal correspondence and OT for cross-modal
208	correspondence in resource-constrained multimodal sarcasm and humor detection (Pramanick
209	et al., 2022). More recently, Xu et al. (2025) formulates speech–text alignment in spoken
210	language models as a linear OT regularization between speech and transcript embeddings,
211	using the resulting transport plan to construct a regularization loss during training. These
212	works demonstrate the usefulness of OT for cross-domain and cross-modal correspondence
213	learning. However, the linear OT formulations are often used to align features with the same
214	dimensions. Gromov–Wasserstein-type OT (GWOT) (Mémoli, 2011) can handle distributions
215	with different dimensions as it compares distributions through pairwise relational structure
216	rather than direct pointwise costs. GWOT has also been popular in aligning tasks, such as for
217	words across two different languages (Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018), and for single-cell
218	genomics (Klein et al., 2024). Our work develops a joint kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein
219	formulation that allows for the alignment across multiple distributions.
220	
221	Statistical analysis for multimodal alignment and optimal transport. Recent
222	work has begun to develop statistical theories for both contrastive multimodal representation
223	learning and optimal-transport-based alignment. On the contrastive learning side, Oko et al.
224	(2025) studies why contrastive pretraining can yield transferable multimodal representations
225	and derives sample complexity guarantees for downstream multimodal learning. On the
226	optimal transport side, parametric sample complexity bounds have been established for
227	Sinkhorn divergences and EOT under suitable conditions. Genevay et al. (2019) established
228	the first sample complexity bounds for Sinkhorn divergences, showing that the empirical
229	Sinkhorn divergence converges to its population counterpart at the parametric rate n−1/2 .
230	Mena and Niles-Weed (2019) strengthened these guarantees for EOT with the squared-
231	Euclidean cost between sub-Gaussian measures in arbitrary dimension, obtaining the same
232	parametric n−1/2 rate but improving the ε-dependence of the constants exponentially over
233	Genevay et al. (2019) and extending the bound to unbounded measures. Groppe and
234	Hundrieser (2024) further showed that empirical EOT obeys a “lower complexity adaptation”
235	principle, under which the convergence rate is governed by the lower-dimensional of the two
236	measures. For Gromov–Wasserstein (GW) distances, Zhang et al. (2024) established duality
237	and sample complexity results for a specific form of quadratic GW and entropic GW (EGW)
238	in the Euclidean spaces, which allows for a parametric empirical convergence rate. Related
239	work by Rioux et al. (2024) further develops stability and algorithmic guarantees for EGW.
240	Our analysis is closest in spirit to the EGW theory, but aims at mapping several feature
241	distributions to a common shared latent space under a kernelized distance, instead of in the
242	Euclidean space. The resulting analysis requires new tools from finite-rank approximation.
243

277	2.1 Problem formulation
278	
279	We consider a multimodal alignment problem with M modalities, indexed by [M ] :=
280	{1, . . . , M }. For each modality i ∈ [M ], observations take values in a feature space X i and
281	are distributed according to a probability measure µi ∈ P(X i ). The feature spaces may
282	differ across modalities. Without loss of generality, we assume our dataset consists of n
283	observations from each modality, {x1k , . . . , xM  n

287	component. When the modality is clear from context, we suppress the modality index i.
288	    We aim to align observations from different modalities into a shared latent space Z ⊆ Rdz
289	that represents the shared information across modalities. Importantly, we equip Z with
290	a fixed marginal distribution ν ∈ P(Z) that can be defined by the user. ν specifies the
291	distributional landscape of Z. The alignment between a modality i ∈ [M ] and the latent
292	space is represented by a probabilistic coupling π i ∈ Γ(µi , ν), where Γ(µi , ν) denotes the set
293	of probability measures on X i × Z with first marginal µi and second marginal ν. Naturally,

295	latent space.
296	    Under the constraint of the marginal distributions of ν and µi ’s, the task of multi-modal
297	alignment transforms to finding the probabilistic couplings π i ’s. Ideally, these couplings
298	should preserve the relational structure of the observations. Since different modalities
299	could have different dimensions, Gromov–Wasserstein optimal transport (GWOT) provides
300	a natural framework for finding couplings that minimize an objective defined to induce
301	alignment.
302	    Specifically, the standard quadratic GWOT aligns distributions by comparing pairwise
303	relational structures in different spaces. One specifies relational functions cX (x, x′ ) and
304	cZ (z, z ′ ) on the source and target spaces, and seeks a coupling whose paired samples minimize

589	3 Theoretical Analysis
590	In almost any application of multi-modality alignment, the raw feature distribution µi ’s
591	are rarely observed directly. We have access only to a finite set of paired samples, from
592	which we form an empirical version of the JK-EGW objective. In the data-scarce regime,
593	we therefore are interested in how fast the empirical objective converges to its population
594	counterpart as the number of samples n grows. This is the central question of the proposed
595	alignment that will be studied in this section.
596	     To obtain the sample complexity guarantee of the objective Sϵ , we decompose the
597	analysis in two stages. We first establish sample complexity bounds for the rank-truncated
598	objective SϵR , whose finite-dimensional representation allows the problem to be reduced to a
599	family of EOT problems. We then combine this statistical bound with kernel truncation
600	estimates to obtain a corresponding sample complexity guarantee for the full objective
601	Sϵ . The resulting parametric bounds quantify how the empirical objective approaches its
602	population counterpart as the number of samples increases, with constants governed by
603	the latent dimension, the truncation level, the entropic regularization parameter, and the
604	spectral decay of the kernel.

Multimodal Alignment Through Joint Kernel Entropic
                                                     Gromov–Wasserstein Optimal Transport

                                          Yixuan Florence Wu                                                yixuanwu@u.northwestern.edu
                                          Department of Engineering Sciences and Applied Mathematics
                                          Northwestern University
                                          Evanston, IL 60208, USA
                                          Yilun Zhu                                                                    allanzhu@umich.edu
                                          Deparment of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
                                          University of Michigan
                                          Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA
                                          Naichen Shi                                                naichen.shi@northwestern.edu
                                          Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences




arXiv:2608.04234v1 [math.ST] 4 Aug 2026
                                          Department of Mechanical Engineering
                                          Northwestern University
                                          Evanston, IL 60208, USA


                                                                                        Abstract
                                              We study the problem of aligning data from multiple modalities into a shared representation
                                              space, focusing on settings where strong pretrained unimodal encoders are available but cross-
                                              modal paired data are scarce. We propose a structure-preserving alignment framework, joint
                                              kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein Optimal Transport (JK-EGW), which maps multiple
                                              modalities into a common latent space by minimizing a quadratic optimal transport objective.
                                              JK-EGW leverages fine-grained similarity relationships within and across modalities to
                                              construct a global affinity kernel instead of relying on raw feature-space distances. Our
                                              framework naturally provides explicit control over the geometry and distribution of the
                                              latent embedding. On the theory side, we establish parametric sample complexity rate of
                                              n−1/2 , matching the corresponding rates for standard, entropic and Gromov–Wasserstein
                                              optimal transport. On the algorithmic side, we derive a scalable alternating procedure to
                                              solve JK-EGW with entropic optimal transport (EOT) updates through a low-rank kernel
                                              approximation and a variational lifting. This lifting scheme effectively relieves the burden
                                              of a quadratic objective, and allowing us to take the advantage of existing EOT solvers.
                                              Empirically, we focus on post-hoc alignment of embeddings from pretrained encoders in
                                              data-scarce regimes, and show that our proposed method achieves improved multimodal
                                              retrieval performance compared to existing alignment baselines.
                                              Keywords: Kernel Gromov–Wasserstein Optimal Transport, Multimodal Alignment,
                                              Finite-rank Approximation, Sample Complexity, Representation Learning


                                          1 Introduction
                                          Multimodal learning aims to integrate information from heterogeneous data sources, such
                                          as images, text, audio, and sensor measurements. Since different modalities are often
                                          represented in distinct feature spaces, a fundamental challenge is to construct a shared
                                          representation in which semantically related observations from different modalities become
                                          comparable (Wang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Such aligned represen-

                                          ©2026 Yixuan Florence Wu, Yilun Zhu, Naichen Shi.
                                          License: CC-BY 4.0, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.
                                      Wu, Zhu, and Shi




tations provide a common interface for downstream tasks (Liang et al., 2024), including
cross-modal retrieval (Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015; Faghri et al., 2017), zero-shot classifica-
tion (Frome et al., 2013; Radford et al., 2021), multimodal prediction (Liang et al., 2021),
and representation transfer (Moschella et al., 2022), etc. Developing principled methods
for multimodal alignment is therefore a basic step toward learning systems that can use
complementary information across modalities.
    A large number of techniques focus on pretraining joint representation encoders via
auto-encoders (Suzuki et al., 2016; Sutter et al., 2024), contrastive learning (Radford et al.,
2021; Elizalde et al., 2023), and auto-regressive learning (Team et al., 2024; Aiello et al.,
2024). To circumvent the need for extensive training data and computational resources,
numerous methods (Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Gröger et al., 2025) also propose to
leverage pretrained single-modal encoders, such as DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025), Modern-
BERT (Warner et al., 2025), or BEATs (Chen et al., 2022), to construct semantically aligned
representations across modalities. We focus on this setting of representation alignment.
    One limitation of these approaches, however, is that the distribution of the joint represen-
tations remains uncontrolled. The geometry of the shared space is largely determined from
the source encoders and shaped by the alignment objective, without being explicitly matched
to a prescribed reference distribution. Consequently, the learned representations may exhibit
undesirable geometric properties, such as anisotropy, distortions, or even mode collapse.
This motivates our central research question: can we construct joint latent representations
that preserve semantic structure from multiple modalities while conforming to a prescribed
marginal distribution?
    We address this question from the perspective of Gromov–Wasserstein optimal transport
(GWOT) (Mémoli, 2011). GWOT constructs a probabilistic coupling between distributions
supported on distinct spaces by minimizing the discrepancy between their within-space
pairwise relations. The resulting coupling therefore aligns the two distributions by preserving,
as closely as possible, the relational structure of the source representations.
    It is therefore natural to extend the standard GWOT formulation (Peyré et al., 2016)
to multimodal representation learning. Such an extension should integrate two types of
information. The first is the semantic structure of the observed features within each
modality, which should be preserved when modality-specific knowledge is transferred to the
joint representation space. The second is the set of cross-modal correspondences, which
characterizes the relationships among observations from different modalities and guides their
alignment in the joint space.
    To capture both sources of information, we construct a global affinity kernel K on the
disjoint union of all modality-specific representation spaces. Consider, for example, an
image–text alignment problem. Within the image modality, an image of a black dog may
have high affinity with another image of a black dog. Across modalities, the same image
may also have high affinity with the text “black dog” (see Figure 1). More generally, we
propose to construct the within-modality component of K by feature similarity metrics, and
the cross-modality component of K by domain knowledge, including class labels (Cristianini
et al., 2001), expert knowledge (Kulis et al., 2005), or similarities derived from pretrained
representations (Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018).
    Building on this affinity kernel, we introduce the joint kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein
(JK-EGW) objective, which formulates joint representation learning as an optimal transport

                                               2
                            JK-EGW for Multimodal Alignment




Figure 1: A global affinity kernel K scores observation pairs within and across modalities.
          Each modality is coupled to a prescribed latent reference ν.



problem. JK-EGW aligns the distribution of each modality with a common reference
distribution in the latent space through probabilistic couplings. The objective encourages
observations with high affinity to link to nearby latent representations, thereby unifying
within-modality structure preservation and cross-modal alignment.
    In practical applications, instance-level cross-modal pairs are costly to collect and are
therefore often scarce. It is thus important to characterize the finite-sample statistical error of
JK-EGW. Establishing such guarantees is challenging, however, because the general GWOT
objective takes the form of a nonconvex quadratic program (Scetbon et al., 2022), whose
global optimization can be NP-hard (Burkard, 1984; Kravtsova, 2024). This nonconvexity
complicates the statistical analysis and the optimization of empirical solutions.
    We address this challenge by studying a specific class of kernel GWOT problems whose
affinity kernel K approximately admits a separable decomposition in terms of products of
basis functions. For a finite-rank truncation of K, we show that the resulting quadratic
GWOT problem can be lifted to a linear optimal transport (LOT) problem whose cost
function depends on an additional set of auxiliary variables. This reformulation makes
the statistical error amenable to analysis using tools developed for LOT. In particular, we
establish finite-sample guarantees showing that the empirical optimal value converges to
its population counterpart at the parametric rate O(n−1/2 ). For the full-kernel objective,
the bound includes an additional truncation term that quantifies the discrepancy between
the original kernel and its finite-rank approximation. Our results therefore distinguish the
statistical error arising from finite sampling from the approximation error introduced by
kernel truncation.
    Computationally, the basis-product structure naturally motivates an efficient alternating
optimization algorithm for JK-EGW. We first construct a low-rank approximation of the
empirical kernel matrix and use it to derive a variational lifting of the original quadratic
objective. The lifted optimization problem should optimize over both the transport plan
and the auxiliary variables. With fixed transport plan, the auxiliary variables admit a
closed-form update. With fixed auxiliary variables, the transport-plan update reduces to

                                                3
                                     Wu, Zhu, and Shi




a standard entropic optimal transport (EOT) problem over discrete distributions. The
latter can therefore be solved using existing scalable OT solvers, such as Sinkhorn-type
algorithms (Cuturi, 2013). Therefore, we can construct an alternating minimization algorithm
by iteratively update the two parameter blocks.
    We evaluate JK-EGW on image–text alignment tasks derived from MS–COCO (Lin et al.,
2014). The results show that JK-EGW learns geometrically coherent shared representations
and achieves decent performance in bidirectional image–text retrieval.
    In summary, our main contributions are as follows:
  1. We formulate joint kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein optimal transport (JK-EGW)
     for aligning observations from multiple modalities into a shared representation space
     whose marginal distribution follows a prescribed reference distribution.
  2. For kernels admitting a separable basis decomposition, we establish a finite-sample
     error bound of JK-EGW consisting of a statistical term of order O(n−1/2 ) and a
     kernel-truncation term. Our analysis introduces a new variational formulation and
     develops techniques for establishing the regularity of optimal transport plans under
     costs induced by the kernel basis.
  3. Building on the variational formulation of the empirical JK-EGW problem, we develop
     a scalable alternating optimization algorithm. One parameter block admits a closed-
     form update, while the other reduces to an entropic optimal transport (EOT) problem
     that can be solved using standard EOT solvers.
  4. We empirically evaluate JK-EGW on digit multi-feature alignment, image–text retrieval
     tasks to demonstrate its applicability.

1.1 Related Works
Alignment of pretrained unimodal encoders. Multiple works leverage frozen pre-
trained unimodal encoders and learn only a lightweight post-hoc alignment mechanism
from scarce cross-modal correspondence data. Early works, such as APE (Rosenfeld et al.,
2022) and ImageBind (Girdhar et al., 2023), align several modalities onto a fixed, pre-
trained image–text embedding space by minimizing InfoNCE loss. Recent vision–language
alignment methods further develop this idea by assessing or selecting compatible frozen
encoder pairs and training simple projectors or alignment layers between their embedding
spaces (Maniparambil et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). More directly related to our empirical
baselines, CSA (Li et al., 2025) maps frozen unimodal features into a multimodal feature
space and uses a weighted similarity score. STRUCTURE (Gröger et al., 2025) improves
limited-data alignment by regularizing the learned representation to preserve the multiscale
neighborhood geometry of pretrained unimodal latent spaces. Together, these methods show
that post-hoc alignment of frozen encoders is a practical and data-efficient alternative to
training multimodal models from scratch. Our work follows a similar rationale but studies a
different formulation of this aligning problem, which allows for an explicitly chosen marginal
distribution on the shared latent space. Prior work suggests that latent geometry influences
compositional and cross-modal generation (Girdhar et al., 2023), robustness to missing or
noisy modalities (Tsai et al., 2018), downstream task performance (Jiang et al., 2023), and
the emergence and impact of modality gaps (Liang et al., 2022).

                                              4
                          JK-EGW for Multimodal Alignment




Structure-aware alignment via optimal transport. Optimal transport (OT) provides
a distributional framework for aligning heterogeneous datasets through learned couplings.
Several works have used OT to improve multimodal or cross-domain alignment by exploiting
structure beyond independent instance matching. For example, hierarchical OT leverages
clustered structure to improve alignment in noisy or ambiguous settings (Lee et al., 2019),
while MuLOT uses self-attention for intra-modal correspondence and OT for cross-modal
correspondence in resource-constrained multimodal sarcasm and humor detection (Pramanick
et al., 2022). More recently, Xu et al. (2025) formulates speech–text alignment in spoken
language models as a linear OT regularization between speech and transcript embeddings,
using the resulting transport plan to construct a regularization loss during training. These
works demonstrate the usefulness of OT for cross-domain and cross-modal correspondence
learning. However, the linear OT formulations are often used to align features with the same
dimensions. Gromov–Wasserstein-type OT (GWOT) (Mémoli, 2011) can handle distributions
with different dimensions as it compares distributions through pairwise relational structure
rather than direct pointwise costs. GWOT has also been popular in aligning tasks, such as for
words across two different languages (Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018), and for single-cell
genomics (Klein et al., 2024). Our work develops a joint kernel entropic Gromov–Wasserstein
formulation that allows for the alignment across multiple distributions.

Statistical analysis for multimodal alignment and optimal transport. Recent
work has begun to develop statistical theories for both contrastive multimodal representation
learning and optimal-transport-based alignment. On the contrastive learning side, Oko et al.
(2025) studies why contrastive pretraining can yield transferable multimodal representations
and derives sample complexity guarantees for downstream multimodal learning. On the
optimal transport side, parametric sample complexity bounds have been established for
Sinkhorn divergences and EOT under suitable conditions. Genevay et al. (2019) established
the first sample complexity bounds for Sinkhorn divergences, showing that the empirical
Sinkhorn divergence converges to its population counterpart at the parametric rate n−1/2 .
Mena and Niles-Weed (2019) strengthened these guarantees for EOT with the squared-
Euclidean cost between sub-Gaussian measures in arbitrary dimension, obtaining the same
parametric n−1/2 rate but improving the ε-dependence of the constants exponentially over
Genevay et al. (2019) and extending the bound to unbounded measures. Groppe and
Hundrieser (2024) further showed that empirical EOT obeys a “lower complexity adaptation”
principle, under which the convergence rate is governed by the lower-dimensional of the two
measures. For Gromov–Wasserstein (GW) distances, Zhang et al. (2024) established duality
and sample complexity results for a specific form of quadratic GW and entropic GW (EGW)
in the Euclidean spaces, which allows for a parametric empirical convergence rate. Related
work by Rioux et al. (2024) further develops stability and algorithmic guarantees for EGW.
Our analysis is closest in spirit to the EGW theory, but aims at mapping several feature
distributions to a common shared latent space under a kernelized distance, instead of in the
Euclidean space. The resulting analysis requires new tools from finite-rank approximation.

2.1 Problem formulation

We consider a multimodal alignment problem with M modalities, indexed by [M ] :=

are distributed according to a probability measure µi ∈ P(X i ). The feature spaces may

    We aim to align observations from different modalities into a shared latent space Z ⊆ Rdz
that represents the shared information across modalities. Importantly, we equip Z with

should preserve the relational structure of the observations. Since different modalities
could have different dimensions, Gromov–Wasserstein optimal transport (GWOT) provides
a natural framework for finding couplings that minimize an objective defined to induce
alignment.

relational structures in different spaces. One specifies relational functions cX (x, x′ ) and

3 Theoretical Analysis
In almost any application of multi-modality alignment, the raw feature distribution µi ’s
are rarely observed directly. We have access only to a finite set of paired samples, from
which we form an empirical version of the JK-EGW objective. In the data-scarce regime,
we therefore are interested in how fast the empirical objective converges to its population
counterpart as the number of samples n grows. This is the central question of the proposed
alignment that will be studied in this section.
     To obtain the sample complexity guarantee of the objective Sϵ , we decompose the
analysis in two stages. We first establish sample complexity bounds for the rank-truncated
objective SϵR , whose finite-dimensional representation allows the problem to be reduced to a
family of EOT problems. We then combine this statistical bound with kernel truncation
estimates to obtain a corresponding sample complexity guarantee for the full objective
Sϵ . The resulting parametric bounds quantify how the empirical objective approaches its
population counterpart as the number of samples increases, with constants governed by
the latent dimension, the truncation level, the entropic regularization parameter, and the
spectral decay of the kernel.

    Interestingly, the error bound has no explicit dependence on the ambient input dimension
of the raw feature spaces dx . The statistical error term depends on the latent dimension

spectral decay of K. Consequently, when the kernel has a rapidly decaying spectrum, the
effective statistical complexity is controlled by the latent dimension and the effective kernel
rank, instead of the raw dimension of the input spaces. This property makes Equation (1)
amenable to align multi-modal data whose raw features are high-dimensional but structured.
    The n−1/2 rate is consistent with known convergence rates for EGW distances with
Euclidean costs (Zhang et al., 2024), as well as related sample complexity results for
EOT (Mena and Niles-Weed, 2019). The main difference is that our analysis applies to a
kernelized feature-space cost, which is natural in heterogeneous multimodal settings where
raw Euclidean distances across modalities are not directly comparable.

1454	6 Conclusion
1455	We propose JK-EGW problem that maps several frozen unimodal encoders into a shared
1456	latent space with a prespecified marginal distribution. Theoretically, when a finite-rank
1457	Mercer approximation of the affinity kernel exists, we can certify the statistical error of the
1458	JK-EGW problem, despite its nonconvexity. Algorithmically, we develop an alternating
1459	optimization method to solve JK-EGW. Empirically, JK-EGW learns geometrically coherent
1460	shared representations and strong bidirectional retrieval on MS–COCO.
1461	    Our study also points to several natural directions for future work. First, principled
1462	strategies for selecting or adapting the reference distribution ν to the downstream tasks
1463	would be valuable. Second, our setting focuses on finite number of modalities. Certifying the
1464	behavior of JK-EGW when M is extremely large would be helpful in large-scale multi-modal
1465	alignment tasks.
1466	
1467	Impact Statement
1468	This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are
1469	many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically
1470	highlighted here.

5.3 Image-text Alignment
We evaluate JK-EGW alignment on image–text alignment tasks constructed from MS–
COCO (Lin et al., 2014). The experiments are designed to assess whether the proposed
JK-EGW formulation learns a geometrically coherent shared latent space.
Dataset. We construct image–text subsets from the MS–COCO 2017 training split (Lin
et al., 2014), pairing each image with the concatenation of its five reference captions. To
obtain controlled alignment benchmarks with class-level structure, we use a class-targeted
sampling strategy. We first select a set of MS–COCO object categories and then sample a
balanced number of images per category. We instantiate this strategy in two configurations
with different sizes of the training dataset: a 6K subset with 6000 training and 3000 test
images drawn from 20 categories (300 training and 150 test images per category), and a
larger 9K subset with 9000 training and 3000 test images drawn from 30 categories (300
training and 100 test images per category). Within each subset, each image is assigned to at
most one target category, and the training and test splits are disjoint.
Procedure. We use MPNet (Song et al., 2020) as the frozen text encoder and DI-
NOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) as the frozen image encoder. All features are extracted
once and ℓ2 -normalized before alignment and evaluation. The distribution ν is instantiates
as a Gaussian mixture model with 20 components. Each component follows an isotropic
Gaussian, whose means are placed along mutually orthogonal directions at a fixed distance
from the origin. This is an informative choice of marginal distribution which does not require
the prior knowledge of of the common representation space. We set the dimension of the
common representations space d = 32.
    Algorithm 1 returns one transport plan per modality, π̂ txt and π̂ img , coupling the training
samples of each modality to the latent support matrix Ẑ. We define the per-sample latent
                                     txt = π̂ txt Ẑ and Ẑ img = π̂ img Ẑ, whose rows are, up to
embeddings of the training set as Ẑtrain                  train
a uniform scaling, the barycentric latent embeddings introduced in Section 4. To extend
this map out of the training set, we train a simple MLP for each modality that regresses the
raw encoder features Xtrain onto the (ℓ2 -normalized) training Ẑtrain . Model selection uses
a small validation split held out from the training set, based on validation retrieval recall
at 1 (R@1). Test samples are used only at inference. The trained MLPs are then frozen
and applied to the ℓ2 -normalized test features, so each test point is embedded in the shared
latent space by a learned approximation of the training transport map.
Baselines. We compare JK-EGW with three most recent baseline methods for aligning
features generated by pretrained single-modality encoders. CSA (Li et al., 2025) is a closed-
form canonical similarity analysis method that maps frozen unimodal features into a shared
multimodal space via canonical correlation analysis. CSA+STRUCTURE augments CSA
with the similarity-based layer-selection rule and STRUCTURE regularization in Gröger et al.
(2025). MLP+STRUCTURE replaces the linear map in CSA with a trainable MLP alignment
head optimized using a contrastive objective (Radford et al., 2021) with similarity-based
layer selection and STRUCTURE regularization (Gröger et al., 2025).
Alignment. For MS–COCO alignment, we pool the aligned image and caption embeddings
from the test split and report purity and silhouette scores using the target-category labels.
Purity measures the agreement between a k-means clustering of the pooled embeddings and

the target categories, while the silhouette score measures whether each pooled embedding
lies closer to its own category than to the nearest other category under the cosine distance.
They characterize how well the learned embeddings conform with the semantic structure.
To evaluate cross-modal retrieval, we report recall at 1 (R@1) and recall at 5 (R@5). More
specifically, retrieval is calculated based on the cosine similarity between the aligned test

These plots visually support the claim that the distributions of the latent embeddings from
different modalities are similar, while embeddings from different categories remain well
separated. For JK-EGW, the embeddings of each class concentrate in a distinct contiguous

6 Conclusion
We propose JK-EGW problem that maps several frozen unimodal encoders into a shared
latent space with a prespecified marginal distribution. Theoretically, when a finite-rank
Mercer approximation of the affinity kernel exists, we can certify the statistical error of the
JK-EGW problem, despite its nonconvexity. Algorithmically, we develop an alternating
optimization method to solve JK-EGW. Empirically, JK-EGW learns geometrically coherent
shared representations and strong bidirectional retrieval on MS–COCO.
    Our study also points to several natural directions for future work. First, principled
strategies for selecting or adapting the reference distribution ν to the downstream tasks
would be valuable. Second, our setting focuses on finite number of modalities. Certifying the
behavior of JK-EGW when M is extremely large would be helpful in large-scale multi-modal
alignment tasks.

Impact Statement
This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are
many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically
highlighted here.

Appendix E. Additional Experiment Results
We conduct an ablation study on the latent dimension d, which is fixed to 32 in Section 5.3. We
evaluate JK-EGW and all baselines at d ∈ {32, 48, 64, 128}, keeping every other component
of the experimental protocol unchanged. The purpose of the ablation is to test whether the
advantage of JK-EGW over the baselines is robust to the choice of the latent dimension.
Tables 2 and 3 report the results on the MS–COCO 6K and MS–COCO 9K subsets, where
the rows with d = 32 coincide with Table 1.
    On the smaller 6K subset (Table 2), the conclusions drawn at d = 32 persist across
the entire range. JK-EGW achieves the highest purity at every dimension and is the only
method with positive silhouette scores, while all baselines yield negative silhouette values.
It also obtains the best R@1 and R@5 scores at every dimension, with retrieval performance
nearly unchanged for d ∈ {48, 64, 128} and lower at d = 32. These results suggest that
JK-EGW learns a shared representation that is effective for retrieval and geometrically
coherent, and that both properties are only mildly sensitive to the choice of d.
    On the larger 9K subset (Table 3), the retrieval gains persist. JK-EGW achieves the best
R@1 and R@5 scores at every dimension and again yields consistently positive silhouette
scores. The purity results are more mixed in this setting, with CSA-based baselines obtaining
higher purity at several dimensions. Thus, the 9K results suggest that JK-EGW gives the
strongest bidirectional retrieval performance and the most consistently separated shared
geometry, while class-purity scores on the larger subset remain competitive across methods.

I wrote `studies/wu-2026-multimodal/extraction.json`, and `uv run raft extract --validate --study wu-2026-multimodal` passes. It has 59 items: 6 methods, 15 equations, 26 parameters, 5 boundary conditions and 7 results. Of those, 17 are flagged `missing: true`, each with a recommended default.

**The study has no experiment defined yet.** `paper.yaml` has `experiment: ''`, and `problem/setup.py` is still the stub that raises `NotImplementedError`. So I extracted all three experiments in the paper:
- **5.1, handwritten digits:** a picture only (Figure 2), with no numbers to compare.
- **5.2, synthetic example:** the curves in Figure 4, checked by their shape. This is the one that can realistically be reproduced, because everything is small and discrete.
- **5.3, MS-COCO image–text retrieval:** Tables 1–3.

**Biggest gaps** (all flagged, with defaults):
- **MS-COCO:** the paper never says how the kernel matrix W is built, nor the values of ε, the low-rank cutoff or the Cholesky tolerance. It also doesn't name the encoder checkpoints, which categories were sampled, the Gaussian-mixture settings for the latent reference, the MLP or the seeds. Any reproduction of Tables 1–3 will be approximate.
- **Synthetic:** the mixture weights of the two distributions appear only as a plot (Figure 3), and ε for the sample-size experiment isn't given (only ε = 0.2 for the truncation experiment). The two parts disagree on how the four truncation kernels are set up.
- **Algorithm 1:** the starting value of the auxiliary matrix, the stopping tolerance, the iteration cap and the Sinkhorn settings are never given. The algorithm is written only for uniform weights and square n×n plans. The synthetic population run and the one-sample run need a weighted, rectangular version; I wrote one out as an assumption.

**Where the paper contradicts itself** (noted in the items):
- The text after Table 1 says JK-EGW has the highest purity on both datasets. On the 9k subset its purity (0.633) is the lowest of the four methods; CSA+STRUCTURE has 0.689.
- In Figure 4 (left), the axis ticks run 2⁶–2¹⁰, but the text says n goes from 50 to 1600.

**Reference check:** `problem/reference.json` has `"cases": {}`, so there were no numbers or page fields to check. I didn't set `verified_against_pdf: true`, because with nothing to check it would claim a check that never happened, and I made no changes to the file. All values from Tables 1–3 (pages 24, 49, 50) are recorded in the `result-table-*` items, ready for when the checker builder fills in the cases. Table 2 and Table 3's d = 32 rows match Table 1 exactly.

**CI checks:**
- `uv run pytest -q`: 337 passed, 1 skipped.
- `uv run raft extract --validate --all-studies`: passed.
- `uv run raft review --validate --all-studies`: passed.
- `uv run raft repro --all-studies`: passed; every committed run reproduced.

Those three `--all-studies` commands only listed `transduced-lm-2026`. The new study's file was checked only by the single-study validate above. I haven't committed anything; `studies/wu-2026-multimodal/` is still untracked.
